n: In this long section of the book, the nation of Israel was confronted with a vision of God, similar to how Isaiah was confronted in {{Isaiah 6:1-13|chapter 6}}.

Isaiah spoke many messages from God about the people and leaders of other nations. These included Babylon, Assyria, the Philistines, Moab, Syria and its capital city Damascus.

They also included the northern kingdom, Cush, Egypt, Edom, Arabia and Tyre. Cush was a nation in Africa south of Egypt. The desert area west of Babylon was called Arabia.

The messages were warnings about things that were going to happen. Most of these things were terrible and would lead to those nations being destroyed. Talking about them caused the prophet fear, pain and deep sadness. It isn’t known if the people and leaders of these nations knew about Isaiah’s prophecies. But the people of the southern kingdom were made aware of them. This was one way that God taught his people about the nations around them.

The prophecies showed that God had authority and power over those nations. The prophecies showed that God’s people shouldn’t trust any of those nations to save them. None of those nations could save them from stronger nations like Assyria and Babylon. The messages showed God’s people that God would bring judgement against all nations. He would bring judgement against their leaders for being proud and causing others to suffer.

The prophecies also showed God’s people that God wanted those other nations to know him. He wanted those nations to be humble. He wanted them to recognise that he is the Lord who rules over all. He wanted them to worship him and to become a blessing to other people groups. Isaiah’s messages invited these nations to trust the God of Jacob’s people as their own God. The messages invited them to come to God for safety and protection. This was a lesson for Jerusalem and the southern kingdom to do the same.

This section contains prophecies of judgment against the nations. By including a prophecy against Judah and Jerusalem ({{Isaiah 22:1-25|Isaiah 22:1–25}}) in the midst of prophecies against the pagan nations, Isaiah emphasized that Israel’s identity as God’s people would not protect them from God’s punishment when they sinned as the other nations do.

- *This is the burden against the Desert by the Sea*: This description of Babylon might ironically suggest that the land was physically lush but spiritually empty. 

- *from the desert, from a land of terror*: (compare {{Deuteronomy 8:15|Deuteronomy 8:15}}).

- *A dire vision is declared to me*: The prophet makes Babylon's experience personal, which strengthens his poetry. The concise language and repeated sounds, like *The traitor still betrays* (Hebrew *habboged boged*) and *the destroyer still destroys* (Hebrew *hashoded shoded*; also in {{Isaiah 33:1|Isaiah 33:1}}), add to this effect. 

- The Elamites lived northeast of Babylon. They, along with the Medes, were major rivals of the Babylonians. 

- *I will put an end to all her groaning*: Babylon caused suffering by attacking and enslaving many nations. The Elamites and Medes likely helped overthrow Babylon in 539 BC ({{Isaiah 21:9|Isaiah 21:9}}).
*I am bewildered to hear, I am dismayed to see*: Through his vision, Isaiah felt the fear of the Babylonian people (see also {{Daniel 8:27|Daniel 8:27}}; {{Daniel 10:16-17|10:16–17}}).
The riders were messengers who reported what had taken place on the battlefield.

- *fallen is Babylon!*: Assyrian King Sennacherib destroyed Babylon in 689 BC. The final fall of Babylon occurred in 539 BC. 

In Scripture, Babylon symbolizes all ungodly power structures, including nations and kingdoms that do not follow God and his word. The apostle John offered hope with his prophecy that all Babylons will fall ({{Revelation 14:8|Revelation 14:8}}; {{Revelation 18:2|18:2}}). 

- *All the images of her gods lie shattered on the ground!*: False gods could not save the Babylonians (see {{Isaiah 46:1-2|Isaiah 46:1–2}}).

- *O my people*: The focus returned to the people of Judah. 

- The Babylonians would oppress (thresh and winnow) Judah, but Babylon would also fall. 

- *I tell you what I have heard*: The prophet faithfully reported what the Lord revealed to him.

- *Seir*: This refers to the mountainous region of Edom. 

- *Watchman, what is left of the night*: Edom's suffering would last a long time. The Assyrians controlled the ancient Near East during the 700s and 600s BC.
These two prophecies are about Edom and Arabia, located between Babylon and Israel. These regions suffered under Assyrian control. Like Judah, they would not find peace under Babylon's harsh rule.
Morning is coming, but it will start another difficult time. The Babylonians are approaching, so night will soon return.

- Dedan was a tribe in Arabia (see {{Ezekiel 27:20|Ezekiel 27:20}}; {{Ezekiel 38:13|38:13}}). 

- Caravans (groups of traders traveling together) would hide in the deserts of Arabia to escape attack. The Assyrians and Babylonians often attacked and troubled the Arabian tribes (see {{Isaiah 21:1-10|Isaiah 21:1–10}}; {{Jeremiah 49:28-29|Jeremiah 49:28–29}}).
Tema was an oasis in Arabia on a main trade route from Babylon.
Assyrian weapons of war, such as the drawn sword and the bent bow, were highly advanced compared to the simple weapons used by desert peoples.
Kedar was a wealthy Arabian tribe with many possessions (see {{Isaiah 60:7|Isaiah 60:7}}; {{Ezekiel 27:21|Ezekiel 27:21}}).
*The remaining archers … will be few*: Compare {{Isaiah 10:22|Isaiah 10:22}}; {{Isaiah 14:30|14:30}}; {{Isaiah 16:14|16:14}}; {{Isaiah 24:6|24:6}}, {{Isaiah 24:13|13}}; {{Isaiah 37:32|37:32}}.

*This is the burden against the Valley of Vision*: The meaning of the Hebrew phrase is unclear. If it refers to Jerusalem (see {{Isaiah 22:5|Isaiah 22:5}}), it is ironic. Jerusalem is on a hill, and people did not usually think visions came from a *valley.* Similarly, Jerusalem was proud of its supposed religious *vision*, but its people were spiritually blind (see {{Isaiah 6:10|Isaiah 6:10}}; {{Isaiah 42:18|42:18}}).

The prophet scolds the people for celebrating the Assyrian retreat in 701 BC. They did not predict that the Babylonian army would later, in 586 BC, finish what the Assyrians could not: the destruction of Jerusalem.

This message addresses the Assyrian siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC (see {{Isaiah 36:1-37:38|Isaiah 36–37}}; {{2 Kings 18:17-19:37|2 Kings 18:17–19:37}}). It may also refer to the people's preparation for the later Babylonian siege from 588 to 586 BC.

- The city celebrated with feasting and drinking ({{Isaiah 22:13|Isaiah 22:13}}; see {{Isaiah 23:7|23:7}}; {{Isaiah 32:13|32:13}}), likely because the Assyrians retreated. Now, a new threat approaches: the Babylonian siege in 586 BC. 

- The people did not die in battle but from famine and disease. The siege cut them off from food and caused a sanitation and health crisis.
Leaders might try to flee, but they would not escape (see {{2 Kings 25:4-6|2 Kings 25:4–6}}).
*let me weep bitterly!*: Isaiah grieved for the victims and the destruction of his people (see {{Isaiah 6:13|Isaiah 6:13}}).
The invading Babylonians broke Jerusalem's walls using battering rams ({{2 Kings 25:4|2 Kings 25:4}}).
The defeat of Judah would show what the future day of the Lord will be like (see study note on Isaiah 2:5–22). Jerusalem would have no power to save itself in that time of disaster.

- *Elam*: Elam was east of Babylon and later helped defeat Babylon (see {{Isaiah 21:2|Isaiah 21:2}}; also {{Jeremiah 49:34-39|Jeremiah 49:34–39}}). 

- The exact location of Kir is unknown (see also {{Amos 1:5|Amos 1:5}}).
*Your choicest valleys*: This refers to the Kidron and Hinnom valleys, which were located to the east and south of Jerusalem.
*to the weapons*: This large and impressive building stored weapons. It also stored valuable items (see {{Isaiah 39:2|Isaiah 39:2}}; {{1 Kings 7:2-6|1 Kings 7:2–6}}).

The people of Jerusalem prepared for war. They counted their weapons, inspected the city walls, and made sure they had enough water.

However, they did not think about God’s plans (see {{Isaiah 13:1-14:23|Isaiah 13:1–14:23}}). They focused on their own efforts instead of seeking the Lord.

King Hezekiah played an important role in these preparations. However, the verbs in this passage are plural. Isaiah was speaking to the people as a group, not only to Hezekiah. This is different from the way Isaiah addressed Hezekiah’s father, Ahaz ({{Isaiah 7:1-4|Isaiah 7:1–4}}).

- *the City of David*: Calling Jerusalem *the city of David* brings to mind Israel’s greatest king and God's blessing on him and the nation (see also {{Isaiah 60:14|Isaiah 60:14}}). 

- *You collected water from the lower pool*: Hezekiah worked hard to ensure a steady water supply (see {{Isaiah 22:11|Isaiah 22:11}}; {{2 Kings 20:20|2 Kings 20:20}}).
Judah’s feasting and disobedience resulted in a prophecy of judgment.

*this sin of yours will never be atoned for*: The people of Judah kept adding sin to sin. Because of this, God would rightly judge and condemn them.

This warning looked ahead to the exile. The exile happened in 586 BC. However, Isaiah was already warning about it as early as 701 BC.

- Shebna's actions show that the people do not trust God to save Jerusalem from the Assyrian attack. 

- A palace administrator had the top position in the royal court (see {{Isaiah 22:21-22|Isaiah 22:21–22}}).

Shebna and Eliakim were two royal officials in King Hezekiah’s court (see {{2 Kings 18:18|2 Kings 18:18}}; {{2 Kings 19:2|19:2}}). Shebna believed the Assyrians would surely kill him. So he planned for a well-decorated burial place ({{Isaiah 22:16|Isaiah 22:16}}). 

Although the rebuke of Shebna happened before Assyria’s siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC (see {{Isaiah 22:19-21|Isaiah 22:19–21}}; {{Isaiah 36:3|36:3}}), it relates well to the warnings in {{Isaiah 22:1-13|22:1–13}} about the later Babylonian siege.
Shebna was building an impressive tomb for himself. It was meant to be a monument. This large and costly burial place was designed to last for many generations.

- *sling you into a wide land*: Shebna would not find a resting place or have a memorial (compare {{Isaiah 14:11-20|Isaiah 14:11–20}}). 

- *your glorious chariots*: In his high position, Shebna lived in luxury.

*remove you from office*: Shebna ({{Isaiah 22:15|Isaiah 22:15}}) was demoted to court secretary by the time of Jerusalem’s siege. Eliakim ({{Isaiah 22:20|Isaiah 22:20}}) was the palace administrator ({{Isaiah 36:3|36:3}}). Eliakim was a true servant of the Lord.
A leader is like a father to the people when he truly cares for them and addresses their needs. In contrast, Shebna was concerned only for himself.

- The *key to the house of David* represents a high position of honor in the royal court (see also {{Revelation 3:7|Revelation 3:7}}). 

- What he opens… what he shuts: The highest-ranking officer has the sole authority to grant access to the king (compare {{Matthew 16:19|Matthew 16:19}}).

*the peg … will give way*: Even righteous Eliakim could not save Judah or David's family line from God's judgment. The people of Judah would go into exile over a hundred years later ({{Isaiah 39:6-7|Isaiah 39:6–7}}).

- The ships of Tarshish traveled the sea between the Phoenician coast and the port of Tarshish in Spain (see {{Isaiah 2:16|Isaiah 2:16}}; {{Isaiah 23:6|23:6}}). 

- *Word has reached them from the land of Cyprus*: Cyprus was the last stop for sailors returning from Spain before their final journey to Tyre.

Tyre was a wealthy seaport northwest of Israel. The connection between Judah and Tyre dates back to the time of David and Solomon ({{1 Kings 5:8-9|1 Kings 5:8–9}}). 

Tyre was near large forests and the Mediterranean Sea. It was a major trade center in the ancient Near East. Its ships were famous, and its colonies gave it great prestige and wealth. 

The city faced repeated attacks by the Assyrians, Babylonians, and Macedonians, and Alexander the Great conquered it in 332 BC. Isaiah not only predicted Tyre's downfall but also warned those whose wealth and security lead to pride instead of reliance on God (see {{Isaiah 2:12-16|Isaiah 2:12–16}}; {{Matthew 11:21|Matthew 11:21}}).

- Sidon was a Phoenician port located to the north of Tyre. 

- Tyre’s commercial network of traders was extensive.

- People harvested fish, crops, flax, and linen along the Nile (see {{Isaiah 19:1-25|Isaiah 19}}). 

- Tyre was a global marketplace, similar to modern cities like New York, Hong Kong, or London.

- Part of the great port city of Tyre was on an island. The island city was a sea fortress, but it fell in 332 BC. 

- *I have not been in labor or given birth. I have not raised young men or brought up young women*: This metaphor was a judgment on Tyre’s colonial ports around the Mediterranean Sea. In the ancient world, reaching old age without children was considered a terrible fate (see {{Isaiah 49:21|Isaiah 49:21}}; {{Isaiah 54:1|54:1}}).
Egypt relied on ships from Tyre to export its products (see {{Isaiah 23:3|Isaiah 23:3}}).

- The Lord had brought this disaster on Tyre ({{Isaiah 23:9|Isaiah 23:9}}). 

- Through trade, Tyre gained wealth for itself and its partners. In this way, Tyre helped create kingdoms.

*Cultivate your land like the Nile*: This difficult phrase means either: 

- that the sailors returning from Tarshish were invited to loot the ruined Tyre; or

- that the people of Tarshish had to return to farming to earn a living, since Tyre was destroyed and trading was no longer possible.
Phoenicia was the region north of Israel. Tyre and Sidon were its main cities.
The Assyrians, led by Sennacherib, stripped and looted Babylonia in 689 BC. Eventually, Babylonia rose to become a mighty empire again.
There was hope for the city of Tyre.

Metaphorically, Tyre was like a prostitute because it was willing to sell anything to anyone without concern (see {{Revelation 17:2|Revelation 17:2}}; {{Revelation 18:3|18:3}}, {{Revelation 18:12-13|12–13}}).

- Although Tyre earned money through dishonest trade, the profits will go to the Lord instead of being wasted. 

- The Lord's priests will receive good food and fine clothing. The idea of nations bringing their wealth to the Lord in Jerusalem is further explored in {{Isaiah 60:5-11|Isaiah 60:5–11}}; {{Isaiah 61:6|61:6}}.

- *lays waste the earth and leaves it in ruins*: There is a play here on the Hebrew words *baqaq* (*lays waste*) and *balaq* (*leaves it in ruins*). The devastation will start with Judah and spread to the entire world (see {{1 Peter 4:17|1 Peter 4:17}}). 

- All the earth will face destruction, including its people and political systems.
Here, the judgments described in {{Isaiah 13:1-23:18|Isaiah 13–23}} apply to all of creation.

The messages of judgement in these chapters are about the whole world. They are examples of apocalyptic writing. They use powerful and scary pictures and signs to describe judgement. It was hard for Isaiah to share these judgement messages. They made him feel weak and terrible.

The judgement messages were bad news for people who were proud. They were bad news for people who trusted in cities that have high walls. This was a way of talking about trusting a government or army instead of trusting God. The judgement messages were also bad news for the spiritual forces of evil. These are evil spiritual beings and the devil.

The messages of hope in these chapters are also about the whole world. They talk about God ruling as King of the whole world. He will destroy cities that are proud. This means that God will destroy all governments and leaders that are proud. He will destroy governments and leaders that don’t follow his example for being rulers. This brings great joy to the people treated badly by those governments and leaders. Then all people will learn to do what is right. All nations will honour God. People who were God’s enemies will be able to make peace with God. They will be able to trust him for safety.

God will put a stop to things that make people sad and full of shame. He will destroy death and will give life to people once again. This time of joy is described as a feast that God prepares for all nations. He prepares it on Mount Zion where the temple is. This is a picture of how God would bless all nations through the people of Israel. It’s a picture of how all nations will worship God as the one true God. These messages lead people to sing songs of praise to God.

Jews understood that Isaiah’s prophecies talked about a time in the future. Some of these messages of hope came true when Babylon lost its power. Some of John’s visions in Revelation are like Isaiah’s messages of judgement and hope. Revelation chapters 19 to 22 make it clear when Isaiah’s messages will fully come true. That will be when Jesus rules completely as King in the new creation.

This section is often called the *Little Apocalypse*. It is given this name because it has similarities to the book of Revelation.

In these chapters, Isaiah moves from his present time into a vision of the future. The language is broad and universal. Because of this, it is difficult to connect the events to one specific historical situation.

These chapters are not meant to provide a detailed timeline of future events. They are not a historical blueprint. Instead, Isaiah uses vivid images to describe a dramatic future world that is both similar to and different from the present.

The vision includes elements of both the old age and the new age. For example, the people of Zion are described as righteous (new), yet they still wait for their full redemption (old). This pattern fits with the New Testament teaching that the future age has already begun but has not yet fully arrived ({{2 Corinthians 4:4|2 Corinthians 4:4}}; {{Galatians 1:4|Galatians 1:4}}). 

Peter wrote that believers were already living in the last days ({{1 Peter 1:12|1 Peter 1:12}}; {{2 Peter 3:3|2 Peter 3:3}}). At the same time, he said that the final day of the Lord is still future ({{2 Peter 3:10|2 Peter 3:10}}). These passages show that the present age and the future age overlap.

*earth … withers; the world languishes and fades*: The prophets often used drought imagery to capture the attention of those who depend on the land (see also {{Jeremiah 23:10|Jeremiah 23:10}}; {{Joel 1:12|Joel 1:12}}; {{Amos 1:2|Amos 1:2}}).
All humanity is guilty ({{Romans 3:23|Romans 3:23}}) and faces condemnation (see {{Isaiah 59:1-15|Isaiah 59:1–15}}). Judgment is like a failed grape harvest that stops drinking and feasting.

Isaiah likely referred to the everlasting covenant that God made with all humanity through Noah ({{Genesis 9:8-17|Genesis 9:8–17}}). The prophet noticed a similarity between the wickedness of his time and that of the world before the flood.
Sin has such a strong impact that nothing on earth can fully make up for it. Our hope is in God. Through Christ, God has made peace with the world ({{Colossians 1:19-20|Colossians 1:19–20}}).

People who once celebrated will now sigh and mourn. They depended on wine for their pleasure and joy.

When the wine is gone, their happiness is gone as well.
Tambourines and the sweet sounds of the harp represent happy times (see {{Isaiah 5:12|Isaiah 5:12}}; {{Revelation 18:22|Revelation 18:22}}).

*city of chaos*: The normal problems of city life will grow much worse. Disorder will become chaotic and dangerous.

Because of this, people will hide inside their homes. They will lock their doors to stay safe.
There is no joy left in the land, not because of an official order, but because the people have no reason to celebrate.

- *like a harvested olive tree*: The remnant will include godly people from both Israel (see {{Isaiah 17:6|Isaiah 27:6}}) and other nations. 

- The theme of the remnant is common in Isaiah (see “The Remnant” Theme Note; see also {{Isaiah 10:22|Isaiah 10:22}}; {{Isaiah 14:30|14:30}}; {{Isaiah 16:14|16:14}}; {{Isaiah 24:6|24:6}}; {{Isaiah 37:32|37:32}}).
Despite the cries and destruction, praise comes from everywhere. Even while feeling the pain of the old world's ruin, the faithful look forward with joy to the new world.

- *I am wasting away*: The prophets knew the emotional pain caused by their people's sins and its consequences (see {{Isaiah 15:5|Isaiah 15:5}}; {{Isaiah 21:4|21:4}}; {{Jeremiah 15:10|Jeremiah 15:10}}; {{Micah 1:8|Micah 1:8}}). 

- Even though parts of the new world have begun to appear, the lies and evil ways of the old world still control people for a time.

- No one can avoid the day of the Lord (see study note on Isaiah 2:5–22). 

- *the windows of heaven are open*: This image is similar to the great flood in Noah's time (see study note on Genesis 7:11–12). 

- *the foundations of the earth are shaken*: An earthquake often marks a *theophany*, which is a physical sign of God's presence (see also {{Isaiah 6:4|Isaiah 6:4}}; {{Isaiah 13:13|13:13}}; {{Isaiah 19:1|19:1}}).

The phrase translated as *host of heaven* comes from the Hebrew *tseba’ hammarom*, which means “armed army of the heavens.” This phrase may refer to pagan gods that people believed were represented by the stars.

It may also refer to angels. Some scholars think it could even include demons ({{Revelation 12:4|Revelation 12:4}}, {{Revelation 12:9|9}}). The judgment described here will reach every part of creation. It will affect both the earth and the heavens ({{Isaiah 13:13|Isaiah 13:13}}; {{Isaiah 34:5|34:5}}; see {{Ephesians 6:11-12|Ephesians 6:11–12}}).
*confined to a dungeon and punished*: See also {{2 Peter 2:4|2 Peter 2:4}}; {{Revelation 9:2|Revelation 9:2}}, {{Revelation 9:11|11}}; {{Revelation 17:8|17:8}}.
Isaiah praises God for protecting those in need (see {{Isaiah 12:1-6|Isaiah 12:1–6}}).

The second part of the Little Apocalypse (see study note on Isaiah 24:1–27:13) describes praise for God's judgment ({{Isaiah 25:1-5|Isaiah 25:1–5}}, {{Isaiah 25:11-12|11–12}}) and salvation ({{Isaiah 25:6-9|25:6–9}}).
Assyria and Egypt were strong and ruthless nations, but in the future, they will honor God instead of their own power.

*On this mountain:* This means the mountain of the Lord (see {{Isaiah 2:2|Isaiah 2:2}}; {{Isaiah 24:23|24:23}}). This refers not to a geographical city but to Zion, the eternal city of God (see {{Isaiah 1:8|Isaiah 1:8}}, {{Isaiah 1:27|27}}).
The banquet is a symbol of God’s providing richly for all those who will receive his gracious invitation ({{Revelation 3:20-21|Revelation 3:20–21}}; {{Revelation 19:9|19:9}}).

- *He will swallow up death forever*: Isaiah hoped in God's power over sin and its harmful effects. In the New Testament, Jesus Christ fulfills this promise ({{1 Corinthians 15:54|1 Corinthians 15:54}}). 

- The Lord's presence will provide eternal comfort. He will wipe away all tears (see {{Revelation 21:4|Revelation 21:4}}).
The new community of God’s people will respond in joy and faith. When the enemy is defeated, God’s people will be free forever.

- *on this mountain*: This refers to Mount Zion in Jerusalem.

- Moab (see {{Isaiah 15:1-16:14|Isaiah 15:1–16:14}}) represents the nations facing judgment, those who rely only on themselves (see {{Isaiah 34:5-17|Isaiah 34:5–17}}). 

- *as straw is trodden*: The people would be helpless and dying in very shameful circumstances.
Isaiah used the image of a swimmer forcibly kept under water to illustrate that Moab’s people are hopelessly doomed and their human pride will be conquered.

- The *city* refers to Zion, the eternal city of God, where the Lord is present to protect and bless his people (see {{Isaiah 1:8|Isaiah 1:8}}, {{Isaiah 1:27|27}}; see also {{Psalm 46:1-11|Psalm 46}}). Zion stands in direct contrast with the "fortified towns" of the nations ({{Isaiah 25:2|Isaiah 25:2}}; {{Isaiah 26:5|26:5}}), which are helpless and reduced to "a heap of rubble." 

- The walls of God's salvation protectively enclose his people. No one can harm them again.
The new community of God’s people is likened to the citizens of a city, securely held together by the Lord. They are righteous, faithful, peaceful, and trusting.
This part of the Little Apocalypse (see study note on Isaiah 24:1–27:13) is a song of praise and a prayer for salvation.
Open access is given to all who, like God and his Messiah, are righteous and faithful. The citizens of true Zion are committed to the Lord.
A perfect peace, marked by harmony, quietness, and confidence, is a benefit of the new creation.
Proud and arrogant people often praise themselves (see {{Isaiah 2:11-12|Isaiah 2:11–12}}), but God humbles them.
Justice finally occurs when the needy walk all over the ruins of the city where the proud have perished.

God will do what is right for those who follow his path, even if they suffer a bit longer (see {{Isaiah 24:16|Proverbs 24:16}}). One day, they will find peace and honesty (see {{Proverbs 2:8-9|Proverbs 2:8–9}}; {{Proverbs 15:19|15:19}}).

The godly pray for the end of oppression and the full establishment of God’s kingdom. Isaiah encouraged the godly to persevere as they wait for their final vindication and the resurrection of the body.

- *we wait for You *(see {{Isaiah 26:3-4|Isaiah 26:3–4}}): Waiting means trusting in the Lord and hoping for his redemption. 

- People demonstrate their commitment to God by obeying his laws; just saying it is not enough.

God has shown kindness to those who do wrong. Even though they deserve judgment (see also {{Romans 2:4|Romans 2:4}}; {{2 Peter 3:9|2 Peter 3:9}}), he has been patient and forgiving and has blessed them. However, one day, time will run out.

- A raised fist shows anger and a threat of judgment (see also {{Isaiah 19:16|Isaiah 19:16}}). 

- Fire was often an image for God’s judgment.

This verse is a confident expression of thanks for God’s blessings. In Isaiah’s time, during King Hezekiah’s prosperous reign, the borders of the nation of Israel were extended, and people gave glory to God for his great deeds.

While waiting for God's salvation ({{Isaiah 26:1|Isaiah 26:1}}), the faithful were in distress and longed for justice. They prayed under the weight of God's discipline. During Hezekiah's time, Judah was in distress when Sennacherib attacked and destroyed the entire nation except for Jerusalem.
The image of a pregnant woman in childbirth shows the nation's pain when Assyrian King Sennacherib attacked in 701 BC (see {{Isaiah 37:3|Isaiah 37:3}}).
Only God can give salvation and bring life (see {{Isaiah 59:9-15|Isaiah 59:9–15}}).

*Your dead will live*: There is hope for the remnant. Some hold the minimal interpretation that this means the people would be restored to the land after the exile in Babylon (see {{Ezekiel 37:11-12|Ezekiel 37:11–12}}) or that the Lord would preserve Jerusalem (see {{Isaiah 29:4|Isaiah 29:4}}, {{Isaiah 29:6-8|6–8}}). 

More likely, it refers to the resurrection of the body from the grave (see {{Isaiah 25:7-8|Isaiah 25:7–8}}). The Old Testament says little about the resurrection, but this text anticipates more detailed discussion in the New Testament (see {{1 Corinthians 15:12-58|1 Corinthians 15:12–58}}).
God will punish the wicked, so the faithful should go home and avoid trouble.
The wicked hold power now, but their oppressive rule will end on the day of the Lord's wrath. On that day, he will punish them for their sins.

Israel used the image of Leviathan to represent evil powers that oppose God. Leviathan's death symbolizes the end of evil, Satan, demons, and forces hostile to God (see {{Isaiah 51:9|Isaiah 51:9}}; {{Psalm 74:14|Psalms 74:14}}; {{Psalm 104:7-9|104:7–9}}, {{Psalm 104:26|26}}; see also the serpent in {{Genesis 3:1-24|Genesis 3}}; {{Revelation 12:1-18|Revelation 12}}; {{Revelation 13:1-18|13}}; {{Revelation 16:13|16:13}}; {{Revelation 20:2|20:2}}, {{Revelation 20:10|10}}).
In the Song of the Fruitful Vineyard, the vineyard represents God’s people (compare {{Isaiah 5:1-7|Isaiah 5:1–7}}).

- God calls himself the Lord of the covenant to assure his people that his words and actions are trustworthy (see {{Exodus 6:2-3|Exodus 6:2–3}}). This phrase appears many times in Isaiah. 

- *keeper … water … guard*: The Lord will give even greater care and protection to his ultimate vineyard than he did to Israel, his first vineyard (see {{Isaiah 5:1-2|Isaiah 5:1–2}}).

- God wants everyone to turn to him and trust him for help. 

- God offers his people a chance to make peace with him.

- Jacob’s descendants will grow, and the remaining people will increase ({{Isaiah 37:31|Isaiah 37:31}}; see also {{Isaiah 5:24|5:24}}; {{Isaiah 14:30|14:30}}; for application to the Messiah, see {{Isaiah 11:1|11:1}}, {{Isaiah 11:10|10}}). 

- *fill the whole world*: This prophecy goes beyond Israel's return from exile to the second coming of the Lord Jesus. It includes all righteous children of God (Jews and non-Jews) who suffer but stay obedient while waiting for complete redemption (see {{Isaiah 26:18|Isaiah 26:18}}; {{John 15:1-8|John 15:1–8}}).
Even though Israel was God's chosen people, they faced punishment like other wicked nations. However, Israel was not entirely destroyed. A small remnant survived.

Isaiah reminded readers of the reasons for the exile and judgment: 

- Israel’s sinfulness, 

- God’s righteous judgment, and 

- the absence of divine compassion.

- The Assyrians forced many people from the northern kingdom of Israel into exile when Samaria fell in 722 BC. The Babylonians exiled many from Judah between 605 and 586 BC. 

- Storms from the east were famous for their destructive effects (see {{Job 27:21|Job 27:21}}; {{Job 38:24|38:24}}; {{Jeremiah 4:11|Jeremiah 4:11}}).

- God's justice requires him to punish sin to correct behavior and purify. The exile in Babylon happened to cleanse Israel's wickedness and remove all of Israel's sins (see {{Romans 11:27|Romans 11:27}}). 

- This aimed to end all pagan worship in Israel, including the incense altars and the poles used for worshiping the goddess Asherah.
Places previously associated with human power and accomplishment would be ruined to the extent that animals would graze in them.

The people were living outside God’s covenant care (his special promise relationship with them). They had turned away from him.

This was a foolish choice. They rejected the protection and blessing that came from belonging to God.

- God's withholding of mercy from Israel ({{Isaiah 27:11|Isaiah 27:11}}) will be temporary. 

- *from the flowing Euphrates to the Wadi of Egypt*: God's remnant will return from Assyria and Egypt to the land God promised to Abraham ({{Genesis 15:18|Genesis 15:18}}; see {{1 Kings 4:21|1 Kings 4:21}}).
The great ram’s horn was blown to gather the people. Its loud sound called them together (see {{Matthew 24:31|Matthew 24:31}}).

- The drunkards of Israel showed pride, spiritual laziness, and disrespect for God and his commands. 

- Unlike Jerusalem, Samaria was in a fertile valley.
The glory of Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, is here contrasted with the glory of the Lord. This section represents the first of the six woes (*Woe to...*).

This section is connected by a series of six threats of judgment or woes (compare {{Isaiah 5:8-23|Isaiah 5:8–23}}). After the initial address to Samaria in {{Isaiah 28:1-13|Isaiah 28:1–13}}, the rest of the section addresses Judah. This is mainly because Judah tends to trust Egypt to save them from Assyria ({{Isaiah 30:2|Isaiah 30:2}}).

More of Isaiah’s messages of judgement and hope are recorded in these chapters. These judgement messages were against the northern kingdom, the southern kingdom and other nations. The main problem was that God’s people didn’t have respect for the Lord. They didn’t worship only God but also worshipped false gods.

God wanted to be their Teacher but they didn’t listen to his teachings. They made fun of God’s rules instead of obeying the Mount Sinai covenant. They wanted peace and rest but didn’t ask God for help when enemies attacked them. Instead they trusted other nations like Egypt to protect them.

Because of all this God would allow the covenant curses to come to his people. He would use other nations to bring his judgement against them. Later he would punish those other nations for being proud. Isaiah urged God’s people to return to the Lord. This meant to turn away from their sin and repent. It meant obeying God and doing what was fair and right. By doing this, God’s people would find peace and rest.

Peace and rest were part of the messages of hope. The messages of hope described a wonderful time in the future. God would be honoured and respected and his people would enjoy the covenant blessings. The Holy Spirit would be poured out on God’s people. That described how close they would be to God. God would be present with them and everyone would see God’s glory and beauty. People’s bodies would be healed and made strong. They would be safe and protected. They would have everything they needed to live well. They would live as wise and holy people who had respect for God.

The story about Assyria attacking Jerusalem is an example of what Isaiah’s prophecies were about. This story is also recorded in 2 Kings chapters 18 to 20 and in 2 Chronicles chapter 32. Assyria was God’s tool for bringing judgement against the southern kingdom. But Assyria’s leaders were proud and made fun of God. King Hezekiah and Jerusalem’s leaders made themselves humble. They cried out to God to save them. God saved them from the Assyrian army. The southern kingdom had peace and rest. But Isaiah’s messages of hope weren’t completely fulfilled at that time. Isaiah announced that one day Babylon would take control of the southern kingdom.

- *the Lord has one who is*: The covenant God will act against his own people, whose behavior had effectively disqualified them as God’s people (see {{Hosea 1:9|Hosea 1:9}}). 

- *one who is strong and mighty*: This refers to the Assyrians, who destroyed Samaria in 722 BC.

In the future, after God’s judgment has purged his people, he will restore a righteous remnant, transforming the desires and character of his people. Samaria will no longer be the source of Israel’s pride. Instead, they will glory in the Lord, their true crown.

- The priests and prophets led the people astray. 

- Intoxicating beverages such as wine and alcohol were prohibited for priests while fulfilling their duties ({{Leviticus 10:9|Leviticus 10:9}}).
The focus shifts back to the unfortunate current situation in Israel (and Judah). The leaders and people will be trapped by their own plans.
The people had become resistant to God's message ({{1 Corinthians 14:21|1 Corinthians 14:21}}).

- God will communicate through situations like hardship, exile, and death to reach his stubborn people. 

- *foreign tongues*: In the New Testament, Paul used this text to describe the spiritual gift of tongues as a sign of judgment for unbelievers (see {{1 Corinthians 14:21-22|1 Corinthians 14:21–22}}).

If his people had listened, God's revelation would have led them to rest (see {{Isaiah 48:18-19|Isaiah 48:18–19}}). However, they did not listen because of their stubborn hearts ({{Isaiah 65:12|Isaiah 65:12}}).

*line on line, line on line; a little here, a little there*: The Hebrew text is hard to understand. The words might be intentional nonsense to illustrate the point that the people were so spiritually blind that God’s clearest revelation was nonsense to them (see {{Isaiah 6:9-10|Isaiah 6:9–10}}).
After giving judgment on Samaria ({{Isaiah 28:1-13|Isaiah 28:1–13}}), Isaiah now judges Jerusalem. He accuses Judah's leaders of being as blind as those in Israel's northern kingdom.

- *have made a covenant with death … fashioned an agreement with Sheol*: There are two possible interpretations: 

- The people had pledged themselves to the Canaanite god of death, Mot, for his supposed protection. 

- The prophet was sarcastic. The people believed their political and economic actions ensured their safety, but they had actually harmed themselves. 

- *lies … and falsehood*: The leaders did not see themselves as deceptive, but they were.

The Lord is the dependable *cornerstone* in Jerusalem, a valuable foundation stone of God's true city. There would be real hope in Jerusalem if the leaders and people turned to Him. By trusting in God, they would be safe during the worst storm or earthquake (see {{Isaiah 8:14|Isaiah 8:14}}; {{Psalm 118:22|Psalm 118:22}}; {{Matthew 7:24-27|Matthew 7:24–27}}; {{Matthew 21:42|21:42}}; see the application to Jesus Christ, {{Romans 9:33|Romans 9:33}}; {{Romans 10:11|10:11}}; {{1 Corinthians 3:11|1 Corinthians 3:11}}; {{Ephesians 2:20|Ephesians 2:20}}; {{1 Peter 2:4-7|1 Peter 2:4–7}}).
The Lord judges people based on their actions, which show if they have true faith (for justice and righteousness, see {{Isaiah 1:21-23|Isaiah 1:21–23}}).
*the bed … the blanket*: The leaders were not ready for God's judgment.

- *as at Mount Perazim*: See {{2 Samuel 5:20|2 Samuel 5:20}}.

- God rescued Israel with a hailstorm at Gibeon ({{Joshua 10:10-12|Joshua 10:10–12}}), but now he would oppose them.
*Listen*: he analogy that follows was written as a wisdom poem, with Isaiah calling on his audience to pay careful attention and to discern what is right.
A farmer knows that there are right and wrong ways to do things, but the leaders of Judah were not that intelligent.
The Lord uses different tools, such as a heavy sledge or a light stick, to achieve his goals. There are different levels of judgment.
*it is not endlessly threshed*: This process would end. After judgment would come redemption.
*wonderful in counsel* (see {{Isaiah 9:6|Isaiah 9:6}}): God’s people should learn wisdom about God’s ways, as the farmer has done.
*Ariel* was another name for Mount Zion ({{Isaiah 29:8|Isaiah 29:8}}). It likely means "altar of God."
During the Assyrian siege, the Lord would fight for Jerusalem. He would eventually make the Assyrians leave the city.
This is the second of the six woes (*Woe …*).
The Lord himself would come against Jerusalem, surrounding and attacking it.
God aimed to destroy the sinful pride of Jerusalem's people. Their voices would rise as if from the grave. Through the Assyrians, God would humble his people, but he would not abandon them.

- *you will be visited*: God will rescue his people. 

- *thunder and earthquake … tempest and consuming flame of fire*: These events describe a theophany (a visible appearance of God; see study note on Isaiah 5:25).
The Assyrians suddenly ended the siege, as if in a dream or a vision in the night. God would save Judah and judge Assyria.
Like a hungry or thirsty person, the Assyrians could taste the victory over Jerusalem. Yet they never became victorious.

Jerusalem’s blindness kept its people from understanding God’s plan.

Here, *blindness* does not mean physical blindness. It means spiritual blindness. The people could see with their eyes, but they did not understand what God was doing.

- *a spirit of deep sleep*: God reinforced the people's foolishness as a judgment on them (compare {{Romans 1:24-32|Romans 1:24–32}}; {{Romans 11:8|11:8}}). They could not see reality. 

- People sometimes called prophets visionaries. Neither the people nor their prophets understood what God was doing ({{Isaiah 6:9-10|Isaiah 6:9–10}}).

- These people used religious language in their prayers and conversations (see {{Matthew 15:8|Matthew 15:8}}; {{Mark 7:6-7|Mark 7:6–7}}), but they did not truly honor God. 

- In their hearts, they were not committed to the Lord. 

- In their worship, they followed human rules and regulations instead of God's word.

Human wisdom and intelligence will disappear (see {{1 Corinthians 1:19|1 Corinthians 1:19}}). The prophet had already spoken about the failure of Egypt’s wise men ({{Isaiah 19:11-12|Isaiah 19:11–12}}). Even Judah’s wise men would make mistakes.

- Their plans might refer to the advice that royal counselors were giving Hezekiah, who at first attempted to free himself from Assyria by making alliances with Egypt (in 715 or 701 BC). 

- The people secretly planned evil deeds, but God saw everything.

This threat of coming judgment is the third of the six woes (see study note on Isaiah 28:1–33:24). It begins with judgment but moves to a vision of creation being renewed and of the wicked coming to an end.

- *potter … clay*: This picture shows that the Lord has full authority over his creation. A potter has the right to shape clay as he chooses. In the same way, God has the right to guide and rule his people.

Scripture does not forbid people from asking God honest and difficult questions. However, it does not allow people to resist or reject God’s will (see {{Isaiah 10:15|Isaiah 10:15}}; {{Isaiah 45:9|45:9}}; {{Isaiah 64:8|64:8}}; {{Romans 9:20|Romans 9:20}}). 

- *He did not make me?*: When people speak this way about God, they refuse to admit that God created them. They deny that God is closely involved in every part of their lives.

The forests of Lebanon usually picture rich and healthy growth (see {{Isaiah 2:13|Isaiah 2:13}}; {{Isaiah 14:8|14:8}}). They are often a symbol of strength and beauty.

But here, the forests represent destruction and emptiness. Instead of life and growth, they show ruin and loss.

The people were deaf and blind in their hearts and spirits. This means they would not listen to God or understand his truth (see {{Isaiah 6:10|Isaiah 6:10}}; {{Isaiah 42:18|42:18}}; {{Isaiah 43:8|43:8}}). 

Yet God promised that he would renew humanity and all creation. He would bring healing and new life (see {{Isaiah 35:1-5|Isaiah 35:1–5}}).

The false testimony that led to the oppression of the poor through trickery in the courts of Isaiah’s era would end. Because of God’s work in their hearts, the people would turn from their sinful behavior of the past.

- Abraham was the father of all Israel (see {{Genesis 12:1-3|Genesis 12:1–3}}; see also {{Galatians 3:29|Galatians 3:29}}). 

- Saved from human mistreatment and God's judgment, the people would no longer feel ashamed. Their disgrace came from the failure of what they had trusted (see {{Psalm 71:1|Psalm 71:1}}; {{1 Peter 2:6|1 Peter 2:6}}).
The prophecy of woe, which began at {{Isaiah 29:15|29:15}}, now ends with a prophecy of salvation.

The people of Judah did not follow God's guidance (compare {{Isaiah 11:2|Isaiah 11:2}}). They made alliances that God did not approve. The Assyrian attack on Jerusalem was overwhelming. By allying with Egypt, Judah's leaders showed they relied on human help instead of God. Fortunately, Hezekiah later changed his mind (see {{Isaiah 36:1-37:38|Isaiah 36–37}}).
This prophecy warned Judah not to rely on Egypt. It is the fourth of six woes (see study note on Isaiah 28:1–33:24).
After warning Judah of judgment due to their stubbornness and reliance on Egypt ({{Isaiah 30:1-17|Isaiah 30:1–17}}), God promised to show compassion to his people and defeat their enemies.
*Zoan*: See {{Isaiah 19:11|Isaiah 19:11}}. The location of Hanes is uncertain.

- Caravans traveled from Judah through the Negev and the Sinai Peninsula to Egypt. They avoided the main road along the coast because Assyria controlled it.

This desert region was dangerous. Lions and poisonous snakes lived there. The journey put people’s lives at risk. Yet they were willing to face this danger to form an alliance that would not help them.

- *they carry their wealth … and their treasures*: This may refer to money and valuable goods that Judah sent to Egypt. They likely sent these riches to pay for Egypt’s protection and support.
This taunt was against those who were busy trying to please the Egyptians in order to get Egypt’s military support.

*Rahab Who Sits Still*: In ancient mythology, Rahab was an enemy of the good gods and appeared as a fearsome creature, similar to a giant crocodile (see {{Isaiah 27:1|Isaiah 27:1}}; {{Isaiah 51:9|51:9}}; {{Job 41:1-34|Job 41:1–34}}). By calling Egypt *futile,* the prophet meant it would not help Judah.

God instructed the prophet to write down the vision for future generations. The present generation was rebellious. They chose false prophets' fantasies over God's word (see {{Isaiah 8:16-17|Isaiah 8:16–17}}).
*Rid us*: The people of Judah did not want to be confronted about sin or judgment.

The whole society accepted injustice and lies. People encouraged one another to believe things that were not true.

They believed that Egypt would protect them from Assyria, even though that was false. Because many people accepted this idea, it seemed normal and wise to trust Egypt.

It also became accepted to take land from the poor. Leaders treated this oppression as if it were legal and right.
Judgment would suddenly overtake the people of Judah because they were content with their fantasy world, and they refused God’s path to rest and quietness.

- The people of Judah needed to turn away from their sinful ways ({{Isaiah 30:12-14|Isaiah 30:12–14}}) and return to the Lord to be saved. 

- Trusting in the Lord would bring peace and confidence, unlike their desperate talks with Egypt.
Judah relied on Egypt for fast horses (see {{Psalm 33:17|Psalm 33:17}}), rejecting God's help and risking its downfall.

- *one … five*: This curse is the opposite of God's blessing for obedience ({{Leviticus 26:8|Leviticus 26:8}}; {{Deuteronomy 32:30|Deuteronomy 32:30}}). 

- The Assyrians had taken control of most of the land of Judah. Only Jerusalem remained.

The city stood alone, like a single pole on top of a hill. It was isolated and surrounded by enemy territory.

- A faithful God will restore order to the world by punishing the wicked and saving his people from them (see {{Isaiah 1:27|Isaiah 1:27}}; {{Psalm 96:10-12|Psalm 96:10–12}}). 

- God blesses those who wait. Faithful people do not rush to solve their own problems. Instead, they rely on his power and goodness.

This prophecy of salvation gave promises of hope. It helped Israel look away from their present suffering.

Instead, it pointed them toward the glorious future that God had prepared for his people.

- This was likely a challenge and promise to Hezekiah during the Assyrian siege of Jerusalem (see {{Isaiah 36:1-37:38|Isaiah 36–37}}). If he trusted in God, his people would not weep anymore. 

- The Lord cares for his people's needs. When they ask for something, he will surely respond.

*adversity and the water of affliction*: A city under enemy siege for a long time would eventually face starvation and disease. God did not intend for this disaster to destroy the people of Jerusalem. Instead, it was meant to teach them.
The people’s own ears will hear and follow God’s instructions (see {{Isaiah 6:9-10|Isaiah 6:9–10}}; {{Isaiah 29:18|29:18}}; {{Isaiah 35:5|35:5}}).

One aspect of Hezekiah’s reforms was to remove silver idols and other idolatry of Ahaz’s era and to call the people back to the worship of the God of Israel ({{2 Kings 18:4-5|2 Kings 18:4–5}}; {{2 Chronicles 29:1-36|2 Chronicles 29}}).
The people of Judah would again enjoy covenant blessings rather than curses (see {{Leviticus 26:4|Leviticus 26:4}}).
The Lord who struck his people would also heal them and cure the wounds he gave them.
In this prophecy of judgment against the nations, Isaiah foretold that Assyria’s power would be broken by God’s strong arm, not by the Egyptians.
*like a rushing torrent that rises to the neck*: Assyria’s destruction would be as devastating as their invasion of Judah (see {{Isaiah 8:8|Isaiah 8:8}}).

- *His mighty arm*: This phrase is a picture of great strength. It reminds readers of how God defeated the Egyptians during the exodus from Egypt ({{Isaiah 63:12|Isaiah 63:12}}; see {{Exodus 15:6|Exodus 15:6}}). 

- *consuming fire … hailstones*: Fire and hail often appear when God shows himself in power. These signs are connected with a theophany (a visible appearance of God). They show that God is acting in judgment and authority (see study note on Isaiah 5:25).
*scepter*: The Lord, the true King, would be victorious over the threatening Assyrian king.

*tambourines and lyres*: Instruments once silenced in judgment ({{Isaiah 24:8|Isaiah 24:8}}) would be used again by God's people. This time, they would celebrate the Lord's goodness instead of becoming spiritually complacent (see {{Isaiah 5:12|Isaiah 5:12}}).

Topheth was a pagan altar in the Valley of Ben-hinnom, outside Jerusalem. At this place, some people burned their children as sacrifices to the Ammonite god Molech. This was part of false worship ({{2 Kings 23:9-10|2 Kings 23:9–10}}).
